results.title: Sample size and power calculations made simple
results.content: Background Sample size estimation is an important concern for researchers as guidelines must be adhered to for ethics committees, grant applications and publications. Content The process of sample size calculations, including relevant definitions, is explained and clear examples for different study designs are provided for illustration. Conclusions The information regarding sample sizes and statistical programs should be useful for researchers in order to perform sample size calculations for research projects. Background: Sample size estimation is an important concern for researchers as guidelines. According to the literature, the minimal number for pilot research is 10; hence the sample size for the study was taken in light of this information (McCrum-Gardner, 2010). It is frequently used in undergraduate and cross-sectional studies in health sciences and education due to its practical nature and standard statistical assumptions (McCrum-Gardner, 2010 and generalizability should consider more advanced power analysis methods to determine the optimal sample size. Power, effect and sample size using GPower: Practical issues for researchers and members of research ethics committees. Aim. To enable researchers and research ethics committee members with non-statistical backgrounds to use freely available statistical software to explore and address issues relating to sample size, effect size and power. The examples illustrate the importance of effect and sample size in optimising the probability of a study to detect treatment effects, without requiring these effects to be massive. Researchers and research ethics committee members need to be familiar with the technicalities of sample size estimation in order to make informed judgements on sample size, power of tests and associated ethical issues. Health care researchers should carefully consider each of the aspects inherent in sample size estimations. Sample-size determination is often an important step in planning a statistical study---and it is usually a difficult one. Also discussed is the possibility that sample size may not be the main issue, that the real goal is to design a high-quality study. Key words: Power; Sample size; Observed power; Retrospective power; Study design; Cohen's effect measures; Equivalence testing; # I wish to thank Kate Cowles, John Castelloe, Steve Simon, two referees, an editor, and an associate editor for their helpful comments on earlier drafts of this paper.

results.title: 3.2 Sample size determination and power analysis - Fiveable
results.content: 3.2 Sample size determination and power analysis. # 3.2 Sample size determination and power analysis. Sample size determination and power analysis are crucial for designing effective studies. These techniques consider factors like desired significance level, expected effect size, and statistical power. ## Sample Size Calculations. * Calculate sample size requirements to ensure adequate statistical power and precision in study design. * Factor in desired level of significance (α), power (1-β), expected effect size, and population variability when determining sample size. * Utilize specialized software and online calculators for complex sample size determinations in various study designs (G\*Power, R packages). * T-test sample size calculation:. + Calculated sample size: 64 participants per group. + Calculated total sample size: 232 participants. + Calculated sample size: 149 participants. * Perform a priori power analysis before data collection to determine required sample size for desired statistical power. * Consider effect size, significance level (α), sample size, and desired power (1-β) in power analysis calculations. * Utilize common effect size measures in power analysis (Cohen's d, eta-squared, odds ratios) for different statistical tests. * Perform sensitivity analysis in power calculations to explore impact of input parameter changes on required sample size or achievable power. + Sample size: 100 participants per group. + Total sample size: 180 participants. ## Sample Size, Effect Size, and Power. * Increase statistical power with larger sample sizes, larger effect sizes, and higher significance levels (α). * Observe inverse relationship between effect size and sample size when maintaining constant power. + Smaller effect sizes require larger sample sizes for detection. + Larger effect sizes allow for smaller sample sizes while maintaining power. * Illustrate power changes as a function of sample size for given effect size and significance level using power curve. * Consider practical significance alongside statistical significance when interpreting effect size and sample size relationship. ### Examples of Sample Size, Effect Size, and Power Interactions. * Calculate adjusted sample size by dividing initial sample size by (1 - expected attrition rate). + Initial required sample size: 200 participants. + Adjusted sample size: 200 / (1 - 0.20) = 250 participants. + Initial required sample size: 300 participants.

results.title: Statistics review 4: Sample size calculations | Critical Care
results.content: Alternatively, an optimistic estimate of the probable impact of some new therapy may result in a small calculated sample size, but if the true effect is less impressive than expected then the resulting study will be under-powered, and a smaller but still important effect may be missed. In addition, the results of a sample size calculation are entirely dependent on estimates of effect, power and significance, as discussed above. The total sample size required to detect the standardized difference with the required power is obtained by drawing a straight line between the power on the right-hand axis and the standardized difference on the left-hand axis. Fig. 2 shows the required sample sizes for a standardized difference of 0.78 and desired power of 0.8, or 80%. The total sample size for a trial that is capable of detecting a 0.78 standardized difference with 80% power using a cutoff for statistical significance of 0.05 is approximately 52; in other words, 26 participants would be required in each arm of the study. The sample sizes required to detect the same standardized difference of 0.78 are approximately 86 (43 per arm) and 116 (58 per arm) for *P* values of 0.05 and 0.01, respectively. What sample size would be required to detect this difference with 90% power using a cutoff for statistical significance of 0.05? (For details on how to handle unequally sized groups, see below.) The process is similar to that for determining sample size, with a straight line drawn between the standardized difference and the sample size extended to show the power of the study. Fig. 6 shows the appropriate nomogram, which indicates that the published study had only approximately 13% power to detect a difference of this size using a cutoff for statistical significance of 0.05. A trial to detect a 4% reduction in mortality with 80% power would require a total sample size of around 3500 (i.e. approximately 1745 patients in each arm). Any sample size calculation is based on the total number of subjects who are needed in the final study. Studies must be adequately powered to achieve their aims, and appropriate sample size calculations should be carried out at the design stage of any study.
